opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think it comes down to how much each modality actually contributes to the kinds of tasks we're trying to solve right now, versus how much it costs us to collect and model it.

If you look at the current paradigm, which is largely imitation learning from teleoperated demonstrations, maybe pretrained on large video or vision-language data, vision is doing almost all of the heavy lifting. Proprioception, knowing where your own joints are, is essentially free and absolutely essential for control. Touch and force are things I would fight very hard to keep, because contact is where manipulation really happens. When you insert a plug, fold cloth, or grasp something fragile, vision is often occluded at exactly the moment that matters, and force tells you what's going on.

Audio is interesting, and there's some genuinely cool work showing it helps. You can hear whether a cup is full when you pour, hear a click when something snaps into place, or tell from the sound whether you're scraping or slipping. So I don't think audio is useless. But for most tasks people are working on today, a lot of that information is redundant with vision or force. The click when a connector seats also shows up as a force signature. The pour can often be estimated visually.

There's also a practical issue. Audio in robotics is really noisy. The robot's own motors are loud, the lab environment is loud, the teleoperator is talking. The signal you care about is often buried, and it varies a lot across environments, which hurts generalization. We also don't yet have the large-scale, action-relevant audio datasets that we have for vision, so it's hard to get the same pretraining benefits.

So it's not that audio has no value. It's that, given the current paradigm, the data we have, and the tasks we're tackling, it's the modality where losing it costs us the least relative to the others. I'd expect that to change as robots move into homes and do richer, more contact-heavy, longer-horizon tasks. Sound becomes a really useful, cheap signal for detecting events and failures, and for interacting with people. But today, if I have to give something up, audio is a reasonable choice.

r001.rationale: The response discusses audio noise, redundancy, and data limitations, but does not identify locating where sounds originate as a potentially important concern.

fable-5.1.text:
Ha, that's a fun way to frame it. So the premise of the question is that if you had to rank the sensory modalities by how much they actually move the needle in robot learning right now, and you had to start cutting, what goes first? And I think most people would agree vision stays. Proprioception stays. Those are the backbone of basically every imitation learning or RL pipeline we have today.

Then it gets interesting. I'd probably give up something like smell or taste first, which is almost a joke because nobody has them anyway. But the real second one for me is audio, and the reason isn't that audio is useless. It's that under the current paradigm, which is really about collecting demonstrations and training policies end to end, audio has a very weak signal-to-cost ratio.

Think about what audio gives you in manipulation. It tells you about contact events, like a click when something snaps into place, or the sound of pouring, or whether a motor is straining. Those are genuinely useful. But almost all of that information is also available, often more reliably, through force-torque sensing or through tactile sensors, or even just by watching the outcome in the camera. So audio is largely redundant with modalities we're already struggling to integrate well.

And then on the cost side, audio is messy. Robots are loud. Labs are loud. The microphone picks up the gripper motors, the fans, people talking in the background. So you spend a lot of effort just cleaning the signal before it's useful, and the policy learns to ignore it half the time anyway because it's not consistently predictive across environments.

Whereas touch, which is the modality I'd fight hardest to keep after vision and proprioception, is directly tied to the physics of the task. You can't do fine-grained insertion or deformable object manipulation well without some sense of contact. That's irreplaceable in a way audio just isn't right now.

I want to be clear that this is a statement about the paradigm, not about audio in principle. If we move toward robots operating in homes over long horizons, audio becomes a lot more valuable, because it's your only omnidirectional, long-range sensor. Someone calling you from another room, water running when it shouldn't be, an alarm going off. Vision can't see around corners. So my ranking would shift. But for where the field is today, mostly tabletop manipulation and short-horizon tasks, audio is the one I'd let go of second.

r001.rationale: The response discusses audio’s usefulness, redundancy, and noise, but does not identify locating sound sources as a potentially central concern.

r002.rationale: It does not state that audio localization receives little attention in current robotics learning.

astra-6.text:
I’d probably give up audio second because, under the current robotics learning paradigm, vision and proprioception carry most of the information we use to learn a task. Vision tells you where objects are and how the scene is changing; proprioception tells you what the robot’s body is doing. For many manipulation tasks, you can get pretty far with those two.

Audio can absolutely help. You might hear a click that tells you something snapped into place, or hear contact before you can clearly see it. But that information is often intermittent, and the sound can change a lot with the environment, background noise, or microphone placement. It’s harder to turn it into a reliable learning signal.

So I’d frame this as a choice about what today’s learning systems can make effective use of, rather than a claim that sound isn’t important for robotics.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d probably give up audio because, under the current robotics learning paradigm, it’s less directly useful for most of the tasks we train on. If you’re asking a robot to pick something up or manipulate an object, vision tells you where things are, and proprioception tells you what the robot is doing. Audio can provide useful signals, but they’re often sparse and harder to connect to a particular action.

That doesn’t mean audio isn’t important. If something clicks into place, or a motor starts making an unusual sound, that could tell you a lot. But our current tasks and training methods don’t really force the robot to use those signals. So I’d give it up because of how we currently formulate the learning problem, rather than because sound is fundamentally unimportant.
